introduction-embrace-the-failure.core: In distributed systems, partial failure is normal: networks drop packets, dependencies slow down, instances die. Resilience patterns (timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, fallbacks, rate limiting and load shedding) keep failures contained and services degrading gracefully instead of cascading.

first_principles.problem: One slow recommendation service makes the whole product page time out.
truths: Every remote call can fail or hang.

analogy.title: A ship's safety systems
analogy.story: Watertight doors, bilge pumps and lifeboats assume the hull will be breached somewhere.
analogy.breaks: Ships face one hazard at a time; systems face many partial failures at once.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Dependency failure invisible to most users.

check.q: What's the goal of resiliency patterns?
check.a: To contain failures and let systems degrade gracefully instead of cascading.

the-retry-pattern-try-try-again.core: Retries recover from transient failures (network blips, brief overload, leader elections). Retry only idempotent operations (or use idempotency keys), only on retryable errors (timeouts, 503, connection resets, not 400s), with a bounded number of attempts, and only at one layer to avoid multiplicative retry storms.

first_principles.problem: Retries at client, gateway and service layers turn one failing call into 27 attempts.

analogy.title: Redialling a busy phone number
analogy.story: Try again a couple of times, but don't redial forever or call from three phones at once.
analogy.breaks: Redialling doesn't double-charge you; retrying a payment might, without idempotency.

check.q: Why retry at only one layer?
check.a: Retries multiply across layers, turning one failure into many requests and amplifying overload.

smarter-retries-backoff-and-jitter.core: Immediate retries hammer a struggling service. Exponential backoff waits progressively longer (base × 2^attempt, capped), and jitter randomises the wait so clients don't retry in sync. 'Full jitter' (sleep = random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt))) spreads load best, per AWS's analysis.

first_principles.problem: After a brief outage, all clients retry at exactly 1, 2 and 4 seconds, creating synchronised spikes.
derivation: Use library defaults (AWS SDK, Polly, resilience4j).

analogy.title: People leaving a cinema at staggered times
analogy.story: If everyone stands up at the same second, the exits jam.
analogy.breaks: Cinema crowds self-spread somewhat; code retries exactly on schedule without jitter.

check.a: It prevents many clients from retrying at the same moments, avoiding synchronised load spikes.

the-circuit-breaker-stopping-the-bleedin.core: A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency and tracks failures. When failures exceed a threshold, it 'opens' and fails fast without calling the dependency, protecting both the caller (no threads stuck waiting) and the struggling dependency (no extra load), then periodically tests recovery.

first_principles.problem: A failing payment provider makes every checkout thread wait 30 seconds, exhausting the thread pool.
truths: Waiting on a dead dependency wastes resources.
derivation: Track **failure rate/slow calls** over a window.

analogy.title: An electrical circuit breaker
analogy.story: When there's a fault, it trips to stop damage, and you reset it once the fault is fixed.
analogy.breaks: Household breakers need manual reset; software breakers test and reset automatically.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Checkout fails fast with a clear message while payments recover.

code.text:
resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.payments:
  slidingWindowSize: 50
  failureRateThreshold: 50
  slowCallDurationThreshold: 2s
  slowCallRateThreshold: 50
  waitDurationInOpenState: 30s
  permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 5

check.q: What two parties does a circuit breaker protect?
check.a: The caller (from wasted waiting) and the failing dependency (from extra load).

circuit-breaker-states.core: Closed: calls pass through and failures are counted in a sliding window. Open: calls fail immediately (or use a fallback) for a wait duration. Half-open: a limited number of trial calls are allowed; if they succeed the breaker closes, and if they fail it reopens. Tuning window size, thresholds and wait time balances sensitivity against flapping.

first_principles.problem: A breaker trips on a handful of errors during low traffic, or never trips because the window is too large.

analogy.title: A traffic light at a damaged bridge
analogy.story: Green (closed), red while repairs happen (open), then let a few cars test it (half-open).
analogy.breaks: Bridge inspections are thorough; half-open probes are a few real requests.

example.title: State transitions
flow: Open 30 s: all calls fail fast

check.q: What happens in the half-open state?
check.a: A limited number of trial requests are allowed; success closes the breaker, failure reopens it.

bulkheads-contain-the-failure.core: Bulkheads isolate resources (thread pools, connection pools, semaphores, even separate instances or cells) per dependency or workload, so a slow or failing dependency exhausts only its own compartment. Other features keep working with their own capacity.

first_principles.problem: One slow downstream API ties up all 200 shared HTTP worker threads, so even unrelated endpoints hang.

analogy.title: Watertight compartments in a ship's hull
analogy.story: A breach floods one compartment, not the whole ship.
analogy.breaks: Ship compartments are fixed; resource pools must be sized and tuned.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Recommendations can use at most 20 concurrent slots.

code.text:
import asyncio
recs_slots = asyncio.Semaphore(20)
async def get_recommendations(user):
    if recs_slots.locked():
        return FALLBACK_RECS
    async with recs_slots:
        return await asyncio.wait_for(recs_client.get(user), timeout=0.2)

check.a: A failure in one dependency or workload from exhausting shared resources and affecting others.

fallbacks-and-rate-limiting.core: Fallbacks provide a degraded but useful response when a dependency fails: cached or stale data, defaults, simplified results or queuing for later. Rate limiting protects services from overload by capping request rates per client or globally (token bucket), returning 429 with Retry-After so clients back off.

first_principles.problem: When the pricing service fails, the product page shows an error instead of last-known prices.
truths: Some answer is often better than none.
Overload must be capped at the edge.
derivation: Avoid fallbacks that **hide** critical correctness failures.

analogy.title: A restaurant out of one ingredient
analogy.story: They offer a substitute dish rather than closing, and limit bookings when fully booked.
analogy.breaks: Substitutes are obvious to diners; degraded responses should be flagged in data too.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Page shows last-known price with a degraded flag.

check.a: When it would hide a correctness-critical failure, such as approving a payment without checking funds.

timeouts-the-forgotten-pattern.core: Without timeouts, a hung dependency holds threads, connections and memory forever, cascading failures upstream. Set connect and request timeouts on every network call, derive them from dependency latency (e.g. slightly above p99.9), propagate deadlines across services (gRPC deadlines) so downstream work stops when the caller has given up, and keep inner timeouts shorter than outer ones.

first_principles.problem: A database hang with default infinite timeouts freezes every API worker for minutes.
truths: Default timeouts are often infinite or huge.
Work after the caller gave up is wasted.

analogy.title: Hanging up on hold music after a reasonable wait
analogy.story: You don't stay on hold forever; you try another route.
analogy.breaks: Phone calls cost only time; hung requests also consume threads and memory.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Downstream stops work when the user request times out.

code.text:
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 800*time.Millisecond)
defer cancel()
resp, err := inventoryClient.Check(ctx, req)   // gRPC carries the deadline downstream

check.q: Why should inner service timeouts be shorter than outer ones?
check.a: So inner calls fail (and can be retried or fall back) before the outer caller gives up.
